Lifespan variation from rates or forecast draws

Source: R/derive-lifespan.R
lifespan_variation.Rd

Indices of the variation of the age at death in the period life table, conditional on survival to age at: how unequal lifespans are, as opposed to how long they are on average (life expectancy). For forecast draws they are computed path by path, like life_expectancy().

Usage

lifespan_variation(
  x,
  measure = "edagger",
  age = NULL,
  at = NULL,
  distribution = c("age_at_death", "remaining_life"),
  probs = c(0.025, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.975),
  paths = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

A matrix or array of rates with age in the first dimension, an mt_draws object, or an mt_data object (observed rates with Poisson intervals, see mt_observed()).

measure

One or more of "edagger", "sd", "var", "cv", "entropy", "gini", "iqr" (one only for arrays and paths = TRUE).

age

An mt_axis (taken from x for draws).

at

Age on which the measures are conditioned (start of an interval; default the first age).

distribution

Denominator of the relative measures "cv" and "gini": the mean age at death ("age_at_death") or the mean remaining life ("remaining_life") at age at.

probs

Quantiles reported for draws.

paths

For draws, return the values of every path, an array [period, stratum, draw].

...

Passed to the life-table calculation (ax, open, k), see life_table().

Value

For arrays, an array without the age dimension. For draws and data, a data.table with the stratum columns, period, mean, quantiles, measure and at, computed path by path.

Details

The ages at death of the life table are taken as x + a_x for the deaths d_x of each interval (the discrete formulas of LifeIneq). With l the survivors and e the life expectancy at age at, y_x = x + a_x and p_x = d_x / l(at) for the intervals from at:

  • "edagger": life disparity, the average remaining life expectancy lost at death (Vaupel 1986), sum(d_x * ebar_x) / l(at), where ebar_x interpolates life expectancy linearly to the average age at death in the interval, e_x + a_x / n_x * (e_(x+n) - e_x) (the open interval uses its e_x);

  • "var", "sd": variance and standard deviation of the age at death, sum(p_x * (y_x - at - e)^2);

  • "cv": coefficient of variation, the standard deviation divided by the mean age at death at + e (or by e with distribution = "remaining_life");

  • "entropy": the life-table entropy of Keyfitz (1977) and Leser (1955), H = e-dagger / e, the elasticity of life expectancy to a proportional change of the rates at all ages (Goldman and Lord 1986);

  • "gini": Gini coefficient of the ages at death, the mean absolute difference between two ages at death divided by twice the mean age at death at + e (Hanada 1983; Shkolnikov, Andreev and Begun 2003), or by twice the mean remaining life e with distribution = "remaining_life";

  • "iqr": interquartile range, the distance between the ages by which a quarter and three quarters of the survivors at age at have died. The survival curve is interpolated linearly within closed intervals (deaths spread evenly, as with the default a_x = n / 2) and exponentially in the open interval (with the mean a_x of that interval).

The absolute measures (edagger, sd, iqr) are in years, var in years squared; cv, entropy and gini have no unit.

The discrete formulas treat everyone dying in an interval as dying at age x + a_x, so var, sd, cv and gini leave out the spread of the ages at death within each interval (about n^2 / 12 years squared for deaths spread evenly over n years). With single years of age to 110+, the standard deviation of French life tables (HMD) is lower by less than 0.01 years than with ages at death spread evenly within the intervals, with 5-year groups to 100+ by up to 0.14 years.

The open age interval matters more for every measure. The life table assumes a constant death rate in it (with the default closure), while the death rate keeps rising with age, so the ages at death in the open interval are spread too widely. Compared with single years of age to 100+, an open interval from 85 gave for French life tables of 1950-2006 an e-dagger and an entropy up to 22% higher (2.1 years for women in 2006), an interquartile range and a Gini coefficient up to 13% lower and a standard deviation up to 4% lower. With an open interval from 90 the differences were at most 8% (e-dagger, entropy), 5% (interquartile range), 4% (Gini coefficient) and 1% (standard deviation); from 95 at most 2%. They grow as more deaths occur at the highest ages. Use single years of age up to 100 or more where possible, and compare measures only between tables with the same open age.

The life table needs an open last age interval (otherwise the deaths do not add up to the survivors at age at). The open interval uses the life-table closure (open, see life_table()); its average time lived a_x is its life expectancy.

References

Goldman N, Lord G (1986). A new look at entropy and the life table. Demography 23(2): 275-282.

Hanada K (1983). A formula of Gini's concentration ratio and its application to life tables. Journal of the Japan Statistical Society, Japanese Issue 13(2): 95-98.

Keyfitz N (1977). Mortality comparisons; the male-female ratio. In Applied Mathematical Demography, 54-76. John Wiley and Sons.

Leser CEV (1955). Variations in mortality and life expectation. Population Studies 9(1): 67-71.

Shkolnikov VM, Andreev EM, Begun AZ (2003). Gini coefficient as a life table function: computation from discrete data, decomposition of differences and empirical examples. Demographic Research 8: 305-358.

van Raalte A, Riffe T, Dudel C (2024). LifeIneq: Calculate indices of lifespan variation. R package version 00.04.09. https://github.com/alysonvanraalte/LifeIneq

Vaupel JW (1986). How change in age-specific mortality affects life expectancy. Population Studies 40(1): 147-157.

Examples

m <- 5e-5 * exp(0.095 * (0:100))
lifespan_variation(m, "edagger", single_ages(0, 100))
#> [1] 10.4904
x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 2015:2019)
lifespan_variation(x, measure = c("edagger", "gini"), at = 65)
